guide_line: Each lab picture has a short tutor hint, one worked example, and practice you can check.
steps: Pick a lab tool.
Open Help and read the steps before you change the picture.
Try the practice. A miss gives a hint. The full answer waits until the third miss.

worked_example.q: A hydrogen electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2. Which series is that, and is the light ultraviolet, visible, or infrared?
steps: The series is named by the lower level. Ending at n = 2 means Balmer.
That jump is the red line near 656 nm, so it is visible light.

similar_problem.q: A drop that ends at n = 1 belongs to which series, and which band on the strip?
similar_problem.hint: The lower level names the series. n = 1 is not the visible Balmer set.

categories.title: Lewis builder
steps: Add the valence electrons. A negative charge adds electrons. A positive charge removes them. Each hydrogen brings 1.
Join each outside atom to the center with a single bond. One bond uses 2 electrons.
Park leftover electrons on the outside atoms first, in pairs. Hydrogen stops at 2 electrons. Most other atoms want 8.
If the center is still short of 8, move a lone pair from an outside atom into the bond. That makes a double or triple bond.
Formal charge = valence electrons − lone electrons − half the bonding electrons. Prefer the drawing whose charges are closest to zero.

worked.q: Water is H2O. How many valence electrons does the molecule have, and how many lone pairs sit on oxygen?
steps: Oxygen brings 6 valence electrons. Each hydrogen brings 1. The total is 8.
Two O–H bonds use 4 electrons. The other 4 stay on oxygen as 2 lone pairs.
worked.answer: 8 valence electrons, 2 lone pairs on oxygen

categories.title: EM wave
steps: Wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next. Frequency is how many crests pass a point in one second.
In empty space, c = λν. Use c = 2.998×10^8 m/s.
Change nanometers to meters before you divide. 1 nm = 10^−9 m.
One photon carries E = hν. The same energy is E = hc/λ. Use h = 6.626×10^−34 J·s.
A shorter wavelength means a higher frequency and a larger photon energy.

worked.q: A wave has wavelength 500.0 nm. What is its frequency in Hz? Use c = 2.998×10^8 m/s.

categories.title: Standing waves
steps: A standing wave on a string with fixed ends fits a whole number of half-waves.
Both ends are nodes. Count them. Nodes = half-waves + 1.
Only those fits are allowed, so the energy comes in steps.
The round loop closes after that same count of wavelengths. The wave has to meet itself.
An electron has a wavelength too: λ = h / (mv). A faster electron has a shorter wavelength.

worked.q: A string holds 4 half-waves. How many nodes are there, counting both fixed ends?
steps: Each end is a node.
Nodes = 4 + 1.

problem.q: A string holds 3 half-waves. How many nodes are there, counting both fixed ends?
problem.why: Both ends are nodes, and nodes = half-waves + 1. 3 + 1 = 4.
hints: The two ends count as nodes.
Add 1 to the half-wave count.

problem.q: A string holds 1 half-wave. How many nodes are there, counting both fixed ends?
problem.why: One half-wave still has a node at each end. 1 + 1 = 2.
hints: The ends stay fixed even when n = 1.
Nodes = half-waves + 1.

categories.title: H energy levels
steps: Hydrogen levels are n = 1, 2, 3, and so on. The energy is E = −2.179×10^−18 J / n^2. More negative means more stable.
The electron gives off a photon when it falls. The photon energy is the positive gap: ΔE = 2.179×10^−18 (1/n_low^2 − 1/n_high^2) J.
The series is named by the lower level. n = 1 is Lyman. n = 2 is Balmer. n = 3 is Paschen.
Lyman light is ultraviolet. Paschen and the later series are infrared. Four Balmer lines are visible: about 410 nm (violet), 434 nm (blue), 486 nm (teal), and 656 nm (red).
n = ∞ is the top of the ladder, at 0. The electron is free there.

worked.q: A hydrogen electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2. Name the series, and name the color of the line.
steps: The lower level is n = 2, so the series is Balmer.
The 3 → 2 line is near 656 nm, which is red.

categories.title: Orbital pictures
steps: An s orbital has l = 0. It is a sphere. A subshell has 1 s orbital.
A p orbital has l = 1. It has two lobes and a flat node through the nucleus. There are 3: px, py, and pz.
A d orbital has l = 2. Most have four lobes. dz² has two lobes and a ring. There are 5.
On the picture, teal and rust are opposite phases of the same wave. The dark dot is the nucleus.
This tool leaves f orbitals out.

worked.q: Which orbital has two lobes along the z axis, and what is l for that orbital?
steps: Two lobes means a p orbital. Along z, that is pz.
Every p orbital has l = 1.

problem.q: How many orbitals are in one p subshell?
problem.why: l = 1 gives three orbitals: px, py, and pz.
hints: A p subshell is not one orbital.
Count px, py, and pz.

problem.q: What is the azimuthal quantum number l for a d orbital?
problem.why: s is l = 0, p is l = 1, and d is l = 2.
hints: l starts at 0 for s.
d is two steps past s.

problem.q: What shape is an s orbital? Answer with one word.
problem.why: An s orbital is a sphere around the nucleus.
hints: It does not have two lobes.
The picture is round in every direction.

categories.title: Orbital boxes
steps: Fill in this order: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p. An s subshell holds 2 electrons, a p holds 6, and a d holds 10.
One box is one orbital. An s subshell has 1 box, a p has 3, and a d has 5.
Pauli: a box holds at most two electrons, and the arrows point opposite ways.
Hund: in one subshell, give every box one electron before you pair any.
Two exceptions: chromium is 4s1 3d5, not 4s2 3d4. Copper is 4s1 3d10, not 4s2 3d9.

worked.q: A ground-state nitrogen atom has 7 electrons. How many of them are unpaired?
steps: The configuration is 1s2 2s2 2p3.
The three 2p electrons sit alone in three boxes, so all three are unpaired.

problem.q: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state oxygen atom have?
problem.why: Oxygen is 1s2 2s2 2p4. The 2p subshell has four electrons in three boxes, so two are paired and two are unpaired.
hints: Write 2p4 in three boxes.
One box gets a pair. The other two stay single.

problem.q: How many electrons does a ground-state chromium atom put in the 4s subshell?
hints: Chromium does not follow the plain 4s2 pattern.
Half-full 3d goes with one electron in 4s.

problem.q: Which subshell is filled first, 4s or 3d? Type 4s or 3d.
hints: Look at the order on the diagram, not the n number alone.
4s comes before 3d for a neutral atom in the ground state.

categories.title: VSEPR viewer
steps: Count regions on the center. Each bonded atom is one region. Each lone pair is one region. A double bond is still one region.
Regions stay apart. 2 regions are linear (180°). 3 are trigonal planar (120°). 4 are tetrahedral (109.5°). 5 are trigonal bipyramidal. 6 are octahedral (90°).
The shape name ignores lone pairs. Two bonds and two lone pairs is bent, not tetrahedral.
A lone pair takes more room than a bond, so it squeezes the angle a little below the ideal value.
The molecule is polar when the bond dipoles do not cancel. The same outer atoms on a symmetric shape cancel.

worked.q: Oxygen in water has 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs. What is the molecular shape?
steps: 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 4 regions, so the electron geometry is tetrahedral.
The shape uses only the atoms. Two bonds and two lone pairs is bent.

categories.title: Ionic formulas
steps: A metal loses electrons and becomes a cation. A nonmetal gains electrons and becomes an anion.
The compound is neutral. The total positive charge equals the total negative charge.
Write the cation first. Use the smallest whole-number counts.
Put parentheses around a polyatomic ion only when its count is greater than 1.
The finished formula does not show the charges. Ca2+ and NO3− become Ca(NO3)2.

worked.q: Aluminum forms Al3+ and oxygen forms O2−. What is the ionic formula?
steps: The charges are 3+ and 2−. The smallest total that cancels is 6.
That is two Al3+ ions and three O2− ions.

problem.q: Magnesium forms Mg2+ and hydroxide is OH−. What is the ionic formula?
problem.why: Two OH− ions cancel one Mg2+. Parentheses are needed because the polyatomic ion is used twice.
hints: The charges must add to zero. One OH− is not enough.
A polyatomic ion used more than once needs parentheses.

problem.q: Aluminum forms Al3+ and oxide is O2−. What is the ionic formula?
problem.why: Two Al3+ and three O2− cancel. Oxide is a single atom, so there are no parentheses.
hints: Find the smallest counts whose charges add to zero.
O2− is not a polyatomic ion, so do not wrap it in parentheses.

problem.q: Ammonium is NH4+ and sulfate is SO42−. What is the ionic formula?
problem.why: Two NH4+ ions cancel one SO42−. Ammonium is polyatomic and used twice, so it needs parentheses.
hints: The sulfate charge is 2−, so you need two 1+ ions.
Parentheses go around the ion that is repeated.

categories.title: Periodic table
steps: The color is a heat map. Cool means a smaller number. Warm means a larger number. A blank cell has no value.
Atomic radius grows down a group. Across a period, radius shrinks.
Ionization energy and electronegativity mostly do the opposite: they rise across a period and fall down a group.
The arrows sit in the margin, not on the cells. They point the way that property increases.
Select an element to read its number. The sentence under the table says the same thing.

worked.q: Li, Be, and B are in the same period. Which atom has the largest radius? Write the symbol.
steps: They are side by side in period 2.
Radius shrinks from left to right, so Li is the largest.

problem.q: Which atom has the larger radius, Na or Cl? Write the symbol.
problem.why: Na and Cl are in the same period. Radius shrinks from left to right, so Na is larger.
hints: They are in the same period.
Across a period, radius gets smaller toward the right.
